ADP Weekly Hiring Jumps to Most Since September

ADP’s preliminary weekly hiring estimate (the NER Pulse) for the four weeks ending October 31st jumped to +95k (+23.75k/wk), the best since the four weeks ending September 26th.

▪️ The four weeks ending October 24th were revised down slightly to +77k from +79k.
▪️ The 4-week moving average rose for the first time in five weeks to +79.25k, the best since the four weeks ending October 17th.
▪️ The current pace works out to roughly +102.9k a month. That’s above the top of the St. Louis Fed’s 15k to 87k breakeven range and far above the Federal Reserve Board’s estimate of under 10k a month.

The early-October soft patch now looks like a pause rather than something more nefarious. The moving average should keep rising next week as long as the next print beats the +67k from the four weeks ending October 10th, which drops out of the average.

This is a different type of episode.

I remember watching Geoffrey Canada on 60 Minutes when I was young and feeling inspired then.

In person, he's a force of nature.

We discuss all he's learned trying to improve poverty and education in America across 50 years of non-stop effort.

We go into deep detail on why he and Brad (@altcap) think Invest America—giving all children in America a 530A or "Trump Account" in which they own a piece of the S&P 500—could have such a massively positive impact in the age of AI.

I hope this conversation gets you thinking. Geoffrey and Brad are clearly on a mission.

Nearly 70 million kids now have an account in their name. Hopefully we can spread the word so more claim them and start contributing. 

As part of the episode, we will be donating our proceeds from our sponsors (Ramp, Vanta, WorkOS, Rogo, and Ridgeline) to a group of kids of Geoffrey's choosing. Thanks for listening and spreading the word.

Iraq says it has re-started oil exports via its historic Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline after a 12-year hiatus (Ceyhan is a Turkish port in the Mediterranean Sea).

The line inside Iraqi territory was sabotaged in 2014. At the time, the Kurdistan regional government built a second line from its territory, linking to the original pipeline at the Iraq-Turkish border (in Faysh Khabur), allowing KRG oil exports while the rest of the line inside Iraqi territory remained out of service. 

Baghdad said the now re-activated Kirkuk-to-the Turkish border portion of the pipeline would pump at 120,000 b/d initially, with aim of raising that to 500,000 b/d at an undetermined future date.

I send around PDFs and markdown files to my coworkers so much and they use their agents to make sense of the world too, so I started using this skill methodology-appendix to make sure their agents could replicate what my agents found. 

---
name: methodology-appendix
description: "Every data-backed report or memo ends with a Methodology / Replication Appendix: the signal choice and its sensitivity, verbatim queries, derivation pseudocode over named constants, the rebuild command, and drift/limits. Appended by default, without asking."
---

# Methodology / Replication Appendix

## Rule

Any report, PDF or page whose conclusions rest on data queries ends with a
**Replication Appendix**. It is a working recipe, not a citation list. The test:

> A reader with an agent and equivalent data access can regenerate the document
> end to end from the appendix alone, without contacting the author.

If a reader would have to ask "which column did you use?", "what date was this
pulled?" or "how do I rebuild the PDF?", the appendix failed.

## Body voice

The body states conclusions plainly. No process narration ("I was asked...",
"on the first pass..."), no self-grading. The first sentence after the title
contains a finding. Everything about how you got there goes in the appendix at
the end, written for forensic recreation.

## When this fires

Always, automatically, for:
- analysis memos backed by database or API queries
- any PDF sent to partners, executives or external stakeholders
- pages presenting quantitative findings
- anything with tables of counts, rates or percentiles

Skip for narrative or qualitative writing, meeting notes, personal memos,
short ephemera, and documents with no data spine. Do not ask permission.

## The six sections

### 1. Header

```markdown
## Replication Appendix

A reader with an agent and equivalent data access can regenerate every number
and rebuild this document from this appendix alone.

**Access required:** <tool/CLI + auth, internal APIs>
**Snapshot date:** <ISO date>. Live-data documents won't reproduce exactly after this date; see Drift.
```

### 2. Signal definitions and the choice that mattered

The most important section. Analyses usually turn on one column or threshold
choice. Name it, name the alternatives, state the impact.

```markdown
### Signal definitions

| Field | What it is | Why chosen / rejected |
|---|---|---|
| `score_a` | Ensembled score | **Primary.** More predictive per <source>. |
| `score_b` | Single-model score | Rejected as primary; kept for contrast. |
| final_decision | Human decision object | Not queried. Known gap. |

**Outcome sensitivity:** switching from score_b to score_a moved the headline
count from N1 to N2 and changed claim X. A replication that changes the signal
column will not match these numbers.
```

Always include an **Outcome sensitivity** line. If a different defensible choice
changes the conclusion, the reader must know before quoting it.

### 3. Verbatim queries

Every query that produced a number, copy-pasteable, in document order, labelled
by the finding it supports. Never paraphrase SQL. Never write "similar to the
above." Add schema notes a replicator would otherwise get wrong: enum meanings,
non-obvious joins, columns that seem to exist but don't.

### 4. Derivation pseudocode

Queries give raw counts; the document has derived figures. Show the arithmetic,
with assumptions as named constants a reader can swap.

```
ITEMS_PER_DAY   = 8        # observed median, <period>
YIELD_HAIRCUT   = 0.10..0.15   # marginal cases convert below observed rate

gap          = count(status = REJECTED and score >= threshold)
extra_days   = gap / ITEMS_PER_DAY
added_wins   = gap * YIELD_HAIRCUT
```

Different constants change the recommendation, not just the number, so they
must be visible.

### 5. Rebuild command

Exact commands from source markdown to verified PDF, plus a visual check
(e.g. `pdfinfo` page count, `pdftoppm` a couple of pages and look at them).
Name the source of record: the PDF is a render, never the original.

### 6. Drift, limits and known gaps

- **Live data moves.** What was mid-flight at snapshot; what is closed and stable.
- **Coverage gaps.** Fields only populated for part of the range, and how tables were restricted rather than shown with misleading denominators.
- **What this cannot see.** Inputs to the real decision that the data lacks.
- **Retractions.** Any claim withdrawn between versions, and why.

## Procedure

1. Log queries verbatim as you run them. Reconstructed SQL is how appendices go wrong.
2. Write the analysis.
3. Append the six sections before rendering.
4. Name the signal choice and its outcome sensitivity.
5. Render, check visually, then send.
6. On revision, update the appendix in the same commit as the finding. An appendix describing a superseded method is worse than none.

## Quality bar

- [ ] Could a reader re-run this without asking me anything?
- [ ] Is every headline number traceable to a pasted query?
- [ ] Is the signal/threshold choice named, with alternatives and impact?
- [ ] Are derived figures arithmetic over named constants?
- [ ] Is the rebuild command present and correct?
- [ ] Are drift, coverage gaps and retractions stated?

## Anti-patterns

- **Citation theater:** table names instead of runnable queries.
- **Reconstructed SQL:** retyped from memory, drifted from what ran.
- **Silent signal choice:** one column presented as "the score" when a defensible alternative changes the answer.
- **Buried assumptions:** constants hard-coded in prose.
- **Stale appendix:** findings revised, appendix untouched.
- **Asking first:** this is a default, not an offer.

Essential expenses are taking up an increasing portion of US household spending:

Healthcare, housing, utilities, gasoline, financial services, and insurance now account for 45.6% of total US consumer expenditures, near the highest proportion on record.

Over the last 4 years, this figure has risen +1.8 percentage points from its lowest level since 2004.

By comparison, these essential expenses represented a record 46.5% in 2010, following the 2008 Financial Crisis.

Meanwhile, between the 1960s and the 1980s, this proportion never exceeded 40%.

In 1959, these categories accounted for less than 30% of total consumer expenditures.

Mandatory spending is eating up a growing portion of US household budgets.

The off ramping we are seeing is not bullish. There's no way to spin that. 

My guess is that this decline still has a way to go. Anywhere from 6-9 months until stablecoins start to inflect upwards again looking at 2022, but it’s impossible to forecast as it will be linked to the progress of AI.

Stablecoins declining is one of the strongest indicators we have for prolonged bearish PA. It is not necessarily a predictor of a bottom, just that things don't go up much.

I think the anxiety right now of self custody, DEXs and CEXs is too much in general for everyone (normal investors and OGs alike). And it is entirely rational. The surface area of risk has increased due to the new powers that hackers have.

Lighter has lost 100M TVL in the last couple of days, and that spook event for a major name will see people continually reduce exposure to perps dexs for the time being. Hyperliquid has lost 8.82% of their stablecoins in the last 7 days.

I don’t like saying bearish things, but I have survived many cycles by being hyper aware of increased risks. You should be employing the horcrux method and making sure you haven't got too much exposure to one venue. 

Once onchain comes out on the other side of this the systems will be almost impenetrable, which will be a very good thing long term, but that hardening can only come with time and by the best security teams reacting to the increasing complexity of attacks and recognising that every layer of the stack can be a weak point.

Perps platforms are still going to do extraordinarily well once we move past the "everything is going to get hacked" stage, and they are still the thing I am most bullish on.

Always prioritise survival so you can continually play another hand.

📊 In October, value added in high-tech manufacturing increased by 17.6% YoY compared with just 4.8% for overall industrial production, a 12.8-percentage-point gap that has been widening since 2024. While China's overall industrial production has generally been growing at around 5/6%, its high-tech sectors have been accelerating. The sector-specific figures are equally impressive with +21.9% for integrated circuits, +26% for industrial robots and +46.8% in value added for manufacturers of specialized electronic equipment. I have to acknowledge that Beijing is successfully transforming its industrial base. China is expanding its manufacturing capabilities in important sectors and strengthening its global competitiveness.

📉 Meanwhile, in October, retail sales increased by just 0.4% YoY. Over the first ten months of the year, total fixed-asset investment contracted by 8.1%, real estate investment plunged by 21.6%, and private investment fell by 11.4%. China is expanding its productive capacity at an extraordinary pace while domestic demand remains extremely weak. While successfully modernizing its industrial sector, China is still struggling to rebalance growth toward household consumption. The prolonged property downturn continues to weigh on household wealth and confidence, while private businesses remain cautious about making new investments.

⚠️ How far can this model go? If China continues expanding its industrial capacity much faster than domestic demand, it will need to find an increasingly large share of its customers abroad. The thing is international markets are not unlimited and this strategy risks intensifying trade tensions with the United States and Europe. The more China strengthens its industrial power, the more dependent it may become on foreign demand if domestic consumption fails to keep pace, and that dependence becomes problematic in an environment characterized by rising trade barriers and aggressive industrial sovereignty policies.

China is demonstrating that it knows how to build the industrial base of tomorrow but can it build an economy capable of fully benefiting from it ? In my view, that's far from guaranteed.

A few people read my recent post as a sign I’m no longer bullish on #uranium.

Nothing could be further from the truth.

I’m still as bullish as ever. This equity wipeout risks delaying financing for the very projects needed to meet future demand. The longer new supply gets pushed back, the more explosive the eventual price response will be.

When utilities start questioning whether there will be enough fuel for everyone, securing pounds will matter far more than the price paid.

I still believe uranium will trade well above $200/lb and that we will se many equities go 10x and more from current levels.

That does NOT mean I think you should sell now if you didn’t earlier. We may already be close to the lows, even with further tax-loss selling still possible.

Canada could take a lesson from Sweden’s ISK system, where investors generally pay an annual tax based on account value rather than tax on each realised gain. That removes the same incentive to dump losing positions simply to crystallise a tax loss.

In my view, tax-driven selling creates unnecessary market distortions. But until the rules change, it makes sense to understand them and adapt.

Being bullish on uranium and being tactical with uranium equities are perfectly compatible.

Podcasts, TV shows, and seemingly everyone on Wall Street and X were celebrating Leopold Aschenbrenner as the new wunderkind, the genius who had supposedly figured out Wall Street and the future of AI.

Now, with hindsight, it’s easy for everyone to see the risks. But at the time, I was almost the only voice on X warning people to be extremely careful with this guy. His returns seemed astronomical, almost illogical. Something about the numbers simply didn’t add up.

For saying that, I received countless hate messages telling me how stupid I was, that I didn’t understand his genius, and that I was simply jealous of his success. Interestingly, looking back at my original post now, I see that most of those comments have conveniently been deleted. Typical X behavior.

I’m not jealous of anyone’s success. I wish everyone great success. But one thing I’m very good at is recognizing patterns.

Only in hindsight did we discover the extraordinary leverage behind those returns. Reports indicated that his fund was borrowing as much as $3 to $4 for every $1 of capital. What appeared to be extraordinary investment genius was also extraordinary risk-taking.

According to CNBC, Aschenbrenner’s hedge fund, Situational Awareness, reached $45 billion in assets at its peak before declining to around $10 billion. Its latest 13F shows just $1.58 billion in disclosed U.S. securities, although that figure does not represent the fund’s total assets.

And this goes far beyond Aschenbrenner. Just look at the latest 13F filings. Some of the most respected hedge funds on Wall Street were loading up on AI-related stocks, including $NVDA, during the third quarter, just before the recent selloff.

These are supposed to be the smartest people in the room, surrounded by the best analysts, researchers, and resources money can buy. Yet many were heavily exposed to the very sector that subsequently collapsed.

That’s the point. Nobody has a crystal ball. There are no saviors.

There is no Wall Street genius who has cracked the market. No AI wunderkind who has discovered the secret to investing. No growth stock promoter selling you a shortcut to becoming rich.

There is a reason not everyone is wealthy. Generating exceptional investment returns consistently over long periods is extraordinarily difficult. That’s how markets work.

Never confuse a short-term track record with genuine investment skill.

Someone who wins the lottery doesn’t suddenly become the smartest person in the room. And someone who delivers three spectacular years of returns hasn’t necessarily figured out Wall Street.

Time is the ultimate test. Not podcasts, not followers, not headlines, and certainly not three years of performance.

AI data-centre: 100% moratorium improbable, modest slowdown likely and it will elongate the cycle (and the selloff has already priced a lot in)

Post-midterm noise has focused on local ballots, state pauses and talk of tighter rules on new data centres. Legitimate friction exists: power, water, permitting and community pushback are real constraints. However, a near-total U.S. halt is improbable as it will send the US into an immediate recession.

AI is a strategic priority; economic and geopolitical costs of freezing buildout are high. Much near-term capacity is already permitted or under construction.

Private land + evolving power solutions (gas, nuclear, efficiency) + international options provide outlets.

No federal ban has material traction; impact is more delay and higher cost than cancellation.

1) Smoother supply-demand rebalancing (less boom-bust risk for the supply chain).

2) Better utilisation and pricing power for compute.

3) Improved credit outlook and more sustainable multi-year spending.

4) Hyperscalers still guiding strong near-term capex; and they will likely become FCF +ve

The aggressive selloff in AI infrastructure names (picks-and-shovels, semis, related industrials) has already discounted substantial slowdown risk. Multiples have compressed hard while order books and guidance have stayed firm. This looks more like a positioning/sentiment reset than a fundamental end of the cycle.

Stablecoin holders are giving up about ~$12B a year in T-bill income . That income goes to the issuers.

There should be a switch into these products but the data doesn't show it happening. Since the August peak stablecoins are down $17B and tokenised money market funds are down $2B as well, so money is leaving crypto rather than rotating into yield.

Part of the reason is these funds sit underneath stablecoins as much as beside them. Ethena's USDtb is ~99% backed by BlackRock's BUIDL and its supply has fallen from $877M at the end of Jan to about $350M. When stablecoins shrink, the funds backing them shrink too.

They're also mostly parked. Turnover is under 1x a month, so the back and forth that makes them interesting for a corporate treasury is still more promise than practice.

Until access opens up they're mainly plumbing for stablecoin issuers & trading firms, not yet an alternative for the treasurer sitting on idle stablecoins.

In TradFi, money market funds are an $8T market. Onchain the yield-paying version is $16.6B, 0.2% of that, against $287B of stablecoins paying their holders nothing. Cash naturally drifts to where it earns the bill rate, so that ratio should be multiples higher.
